chunks: Familiarity with DMMs, scopes, VNAs, SMUs. The question: How familiar are you with:
The interviewer is asking how well you know four kinds of lab instruments and is checking your honesty as much as your knowledge. A multimeter reads accurate steady values.
A scope shows voltage over time. A VNA measures how a circuit passes or reflects radio-frequency signals. An SMU is a precise power source that also measures.
A good answer rates your experience plainly, gives one real example per tool, and has a plan for gaps.
Think of a kitchen job interview.
You say "I use the stove daily, I have tried a sous-vide machine once, and I have never used a blast chiller, but I know it cools food fast and here is how I would learn it."
That is believable; claiming expertise and failing the first follow-up is not.
the supply holds 5 volts until the current limit, then the voltage collapses along the vertical line as the current loop controls.
Always set the current limit before connecting an unknown DUT.
DMM: digital multimeter, measures voltage, current and resistance accurately but slowly. Scope: oscilloscope, shows voltage versus time. VNA: vector network analyzer.
It sends a swept test signal into a circuit and measures what is reflected and what passes through.
SMU: source-measure unit, a precise supply that forces a voltage or current and measures the other.
Calibration: measuring known reference parts first so the instrument can remove its own and its cables' errors.
A skeleton answer; fill in your own facts. "I use a DMM [how often]. For example, I [measured ], and I know it averages, so it can miss fast glitches. I use a scope [how much].
On [project], I [measured ] and learned [ ]. A VNA measures reflection and transmission after calibration. I [have / have not] used one.
If not, I would start by measuring a known filter. I [have / have not] used an SMU. I know it sources and measures precisely, for LED or battery curves." That is the whole idea.

"DMMs and scopes I use routinely: DMM for accurate DC, resistance and current, aware of averaging, burden voltage and true-RMS; scope for waveforms, choosing bandwidth for the edge rate and using a proper probe and trigger.
A VNA sources a swept sine and measures S-parameters like return loss and gain after a calibration; I understand it well conceptually [and have used it for ].
For supplies I know constant-voltage and constant-current modes, and an SMU is a four-quadrant supply plus precision meter for I-V characterization."
